text: Everything in Effect Oak is an Actor. An Actor keeps a Model, accepts Messages, and changes its Model when a Message arrives. That's the whole idea. Let's build one: a rocket.
speaker: am_michael

text: A rocket's Model is how much fuel it holds. Just a number, described with Schema.
speaker: am_michael

text: It accepts one Message: Fuel. A Message is a fact, something that happened: someone fuelled the rocket.
speaker: am_michael

text: Now build it. init gives the initial Model: an empty tank. update says what each Message does: Fuel adds twenty, up to a hundred. Update is pure. It only returns the next Model.
speaker: am_michael

text: To see the rocket, give it a View. View.make takes the Actor and a plain React component. The component gets the Model, at whatever moment the rocket is in, and draws it.
speaker: am_michael

text: Clicking the rocket sends Fuel. The Update runs, the Model changes, and the View draws the new fuel.
speaker: am_michael

text: A Model, Messages, an Update, and a View. But a rocket doesn't just sit there. It launches, it flies, it lands, and at each of those moments it behaves differently.
speaker: am_michael

text: A rocket on the pad and a rocket in the sky are in different situations. Effect Oak calls them States, and a rocket is always in exactly one.
speaker: am_michael

text: Each step of the flight is its own State: lift off, drop the boosters, cruise, come down, land, and roll back to the pad. Small States are easy to draw, and easy to reason about.
speaker: am_michael

text: Update is now written per State. On the pad, the rocket takes Fuel and Launch. In the air, it takes Land. A Message with no rule in the current State is ignored: you can't fuel a rocket in the sky.
speaker: am_michael

text: Some data only exists in one State. When you press Land, Update reads the fuel. Enough, and the descent is safe; too little, and it isn't. That answer lives on the Descending State.
speaker: am_michael

text: The View draws each State its own way, and Motion moves the rocket from one to the next. Fuel it up, and launch.
speaker: am_michael

text: Land with too little fuel, and it doesn't end well.
speaker: am_michael

text: Run dry in the air, and the rocket is lost.
speaker: am_michael

text: But nobody clicked to drop the boosters, or to burn the fuel. So what moved the rocket along?
speaker: am_michael

text: A Lifetime: an Effect that runs for as long as one State lasts. When the rocket leaves the State, its Lifetime is interrupted. There is nothing to clean up by hand.
speaker: am_michael

text: While Ascending, wait, then tell the rocket its boosters are spent. Separating waits, then sends Steadied. Each step hands over to the next.
speaker: am_michael

text: While Cruising, burn fuel, forever. Forever is safe here: landing leaves the State, and the loop stops on its own.
speaker: am_michael

text: A Lifetime can also span the rocket's whole life. Do something when it starts, run as many fibers as you like while it lives, and add a finaliser for when it stops. It's just a scoped Effect.
speaker: am_michael

text: One rocket is a start. A launch site needs a fleet.
speaker: am_michael

text: A Fleet is an Actor too. Its Model is a list of rocket names, and it accepts Build and Dismantle.
speaker: am_michael

text: Each name becomes a Rocket of its own: a Child. The Model decides which Children exist. Add a name, and a Rocket starts. Remove it, and it stops, along with every Lifetime it was running.
speaker: am_michael

text: The Fleet View lays the rockets out, and draws each one with its own View. Build one, and the others make room. Every rocket gets a launch pad and a landing pad.
speaker: am_michael

text: Each Rocket is its own Instance, with its own Model and its own State. Fuel one, launch another: they don't share a thing.
speaker: am_michael

text: But dismantling a rocket is the Fleet's job, and a Rocket can't reach its Fleet. Not yet.
speaker: am_michael

text: Some things belong to the whole site, not to one rocket, like the weather. The Fleet Provides Weather to everything below it, and each Rocket Requires it.
speaker: am_michael

text: Forget to Provide it, and the app doesn't compile.
speaker: am_michael

text: Update can't look at the sky: it's pure. So Launch asks for a Command, an Effect that reads the weather and sends back Cleared, or Scrubbed.
speaker: am_michael

text: Bring in a storm, and try to launch. The rocket shakes, and stays on the pad. Clear skies, and it goes.
speaker: am_michael

text: A Capability is also how a Child talks to its parent. The Fleet Provides a Hangar, and a landed Rocket asks it to dismantle the rocket, without knowing where its Fleet is.
speaker: am_michael

text: That's the whole app. So how does it get on the page?
speaker: am_michael

text: toReact takes an Actor, its View, and a Layer for whatever the root Requires, and gives back a React component. Mount it like any other.
speaker: am_michael

text: Behind it, one Runtime runs every Actor, outside React. When a Message changes one Rocket, only that Rocket draws again.
speaker: am_michael

text: And because every change is a Message, the Runtime remembers every one of them.
speaker: am_michael

text: Every click, every Lifetime tick, every Command result is a Message, and every Message is in the Log.
speaker: am_michael

text: Pick any Message, and the app is drawn as it was right after it, animations and all. The rocket floats back down to its pad.
speaker: am_michael

text: Start again from that moment, and a new Branch grows beside the old one. Both stay in the Log.
speaker: am_michael

text: The Inspector maps the whole app: every Actor, every State, and what each Message changed.
speaker: am_michael

text: The rocket you've watched all along is a plain React component. Motion reads the State, and moves it.
speaker: am_michael

text: Because the View only reads the Model and State, Time Travel draws it just like the live app. Hooks, context, your component library: everything you know from React still applies.
speaker: am_michael

text: Effect Oak.
speaker: am_michael
